Getting started with pnr

Source: vignettes/pnr.Rmd
pnr.Rmd

A CPR column usually goes through four steps: find out what is wrong with it, standardise it, derive what the analysis needs, and replace it before the data leaves a secure environment. pnr has one function for each.

All CPR numbers in this vignette are constructed examples.

diagnose_cpr(): what is wrong with the column

Ask this first of a CPR column you did not produce yourself:

x <- c("0101004007", "010100-4007", "101004007", "1.01004E+08",
       "3102004007", "12345", "ukendt", NA, "1111111118")
diagnose_cpr(x, as_of = "2025-01-01")
#> ── CPR diagnosis ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ! 4 of 9 valid (2 distinct)
#> ✖ 1 missing (row 8)
#> ✖ 1 in scientific or decimal notation: digits are lost, read the source again as text (row 4)
#> ✖ 1 with the wrong number of digits (row 6)
#> ✖ 1 with characters other than digits, dashes and spaces (row 7)
#> ✖ 1 with ten digits but no real birth date (row 5)
#> ℹ 1 had lost a leading zero (Excel), restored by cleaning (row 3)
#> ℹ 1 contained dashes or spaces (row 2)
#> ℹ 3 valid, sharing their CPR number with another row (rows 1, 2, 3)
#> Birth dates 1911-11-11 to 2000-01-01; 75.0% male.

Every value gets one status: valid, missing, scientific notation, wrong length, other characters, or an invalid date. The notes below the problems overlap and are not errors, but each tells where the data has been: a restored leading zero means Excel, scientific notation means the digits are gone and the source must be read again with the column as text.

The report shows counts and row numbers, never CPR numbers, so it can go into a log. The rows behind each check are kept in the result:

d <- diagnose_cpr(x, as_of = "2025-01-01")
d$checks[, c("check", "kind", "n")]
#>               check    kind n
#> 1             valid problem 4
#> 2           missing problem 1
#> 3        scientific problem 1
#> 4      wrong_length problem 1
#> 5         non_digit problem 1
#> 6      invalid_date problem 1
#> 7     zero_restored    note 1
#> 8        separators    note 1
#> 9       mod11_fails    note 0
#> 10         repeated    note 3
#> 11 born_after_as_of    note 0
#> 12   older_than_120    note 0
d$checks$rows[d$checks$check == "invalid_date"][[1]]
#> [1] 5

A modulus-11 failure is only a note: since 2007 the CPR office issues numbers that do not satisfy it.

clean_cpr(): one form for joins

Identifiers rarely arrive in one consistent shape: 111111-1118, or a nine-digit CPR that lost its leading zero in Excel. Before a join, both sides need the same form, and that is all clean_cpr() does. It takes a vector and returns a vector, so the natural place for it is inside a mutate():

clean_cpr(c("111111-1118", "101004007", "1111111118"))
#> [1] "1111111118" "0101004007" "1111111118"

It zero-pads nine-digit values, because birth days 01 to 09 mean that a third of all CPR numbers start with a zero, which Excel drops. It does not validate: malformed values come back cleaned but still visibly malformed.

add_cpr_info(): birth date, age, sex, and validity

add_cpr_info() appends selected information while preserving the original CPR column. Dashes, spaces, and lost leading zeroes are handled internally, with the same native rules as clean_cpr(). Each CPR is parsed once for all requested outputs, including multiple age calculations. Use clean_cpr() explicitly when the identifier will also be used for joins or export:

df |>
  dplyr::mutate(pnr = clean_cpr(pnr)) |>
  add_cpr_info(pnr, age(year), sex, bday)

Without selections, the function adds bday, age, sex, mod11, and valid. Bare age and age() use today’s date; explicit references make analysis reproducible.

df <- data.frame(
  pnr = c("1111111118", "111111-1118", "111111118"),
  year = c(2024L, 2025L, 2026L)
)
add_cpr_info(df, pnr)
#>           pnr year       bday age sex mod11 valid
#> 1  1111111118 2024 1911-11-11 114   0  TRUE  TRUE
#> 2 111111-1118 2025 1911-11-11 114   0  TRUE  TRUE
#> 3   111111118 2026 1911-11-01 115   0 FALSE  TRUE
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, sex, birth_date = bday)
#>           pnr year sex birth_date
#> 1  1111111118 2024   0 1911-11-11
#> 2 111111-1118 2025   0 1911-11-11
#> 3   111111118 2026   0 1911-11-01

Write output_name = calculation to rename a result. Each age calculation has its own reference, so several ages can be added in one call:

df |>
  add_cpr_info(
    pnr,
    primoalder = age(year),
    medioalder = age(year, "medio"),
    ultimoalder = age(year, "ultimo"),
    sex,
    bday
  )
#>           pnr year primoalder medioalder ultimoalder sex       bday
#> 1  1111111118 2024        112        112         113   0 1911-11-11
#> 2 111111-1118 2025        113        113         114   0 1911-11-11
#> 3   111111118 2026        114        114         115   0 1911-11-01

age(year) defaults to "primo" with primo = "previous_ultimo" (31 December of the previous year); "medio" means 1 July and "ultimo" means 31 December. year can be a scalar, a column, or an expression evaluated in the original input data.

This default makes opening ages equal to the previous year’s closing ages. It can also be written explicitly:

add_cpr_info(df, pnr, primoalder = age(year, primo = "previous_ultimo"))
#>           pnr year primoalder
#> 1  1111111118 2024        112
#> 2 111111-1118 2025        113
#> 3   111111118 2026        114

Someone born on 1 January 2000 is then 0 in counting year 2001; age(year, primo = "jan1") instead includes that day’s birthday and gives 1.

For a specific date, use age(date = ...) with a Date or ISO date string. Supply one reference for all rows or one per row. Missing references give missing ages. Use .env$name to explicitly access a caller variable when a column has the same name.

add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = "2025-07-01"))
#>           pnr year alder
#> 1  1111111118 2024   113
#> 2 111111-1118 2025   113
#> 3   111111118 2026   113
df$reference <- as.Date(paste0(df$year, "-01-01"))
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = reference))
#>           pnr year  reference alder
#> 1  1111111118 2024 2024-01-01   112
#> 2 111111-1118 2025 2025-01-01   113
#> 3   111111118 2026 2026-01-01   114

Existing output names cause an error with guidance to rename the selection or use .overwrite = TRUE. Duplicate output names are always an error, and the source CPR column cannot be overwritten.

valid means ten digits encoding a real calendar date, not confirmation that the CPR number was assigned. Missing and invalid CPR values give valid = FALSE. mod11 is an independent checksum and is not part of valid. Choose mod11 explicitly when selecting outputs if you need it.

Age counts completed calendar years, not elapsed days divided by 365.25. For a person born on 29 February, age increases on 29 February in leap years and on 1 March in non-leap years. For a birth date of 29 February 2000:

Reference date Age
2024-02-28 23
2024-02-29 24
2024-03-01 24
2025-02-28 24
2025-03-01 25

age(2024) means age on 31 December 2023 by default, giving age 23 in this example.

Add byear for the birth year as an integer; it is not among the defaults.

cpr_birth_date(), cpr_age() and friends: one vector at a time

Where a data frame function does not fit, in a filter() or inside an ifelse(), each selection has a vector version:

x <- c("0101004007", "111111-1118", "3102004007")
cpr_birth_date(x)
#> [1] "2000-01-01" "1911-11-11" NA
cpr_birth_year(x)
#> [1] 2000 1911   NA
cpr_sex(x)
#> [1]  1  0 NA
cpr_valid(x)
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
cpr_age(x, 2025)
#> [1]  24 113  NA
cpr_age(x, date = "2025-07-01")
#> [1]  25 113  NA

They return exactly what the matching add_cpr_info() selection does. cpr_age() takes the same references as age(), as values, so inside mutate() a column works directly:

df |>
  dplyr::filter(cpr_valid(pnr)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(alder = cpr_age(pnr, year))

Each call parses the CPR numbers again. When you need several columns, add_cpr_info() parses once for all of them.

pseudo_cpr(): a serial number instead of the CPR number

Before data leaves a secure environment, derive what the analysis needs and replace the CPR number with a serial number:

df <- data.frame(pnr = c("0101004007", "1111111118", "010100-4007"), year = 2025L)
df |>
  add_cpr_info(pnr, age(year), sex) |>
  dplyr::mutate(id = pseudo_cpr(pnr), pnr = NULL)
#>   year age sex id
#> 1 2025  24   1  1
#> 2 2025 113   0  2
#> 3 2025  24   1  1

The same CPR number gets the same serial number, also across formats, so a person can still be followed across rows. The numbers are drawn in random order: numbering in sorted order would follow the birth date, and in order of appearance the row order of the source file.

No key is kept, so two calls give unrelated numbers. To link several tables, pseudonymise them in one call or join first. Use seed to get the same numbering again on exactly the same input:

pseudo_cpr(c("0101004007", "1111111118", "010100-4007"), seed = 1)
#> [1] 1 2 1

A serial number makes the data pseudonymous, not anonymous: birth date, sex and other columns can still single out a person.
